rules.statement: After an interactive sign-in or logout, redirect only to a `ReturnUrl` that the server has validated as a local URL on the OP's own origin; never redirect to an unvalidated caller-supplied URL.
rules.why: The login POST sets the session cookie and must honor a server-validated same-origin `ReturnUrl`, so an unvalidated redirect would make it an open redirect.
rules.check: Look for `Redirect(returnUrl)` or similar in login, logout and consent handlers without `Url.IsLocalUrl`, `LocalRedirect` or an equivalent same-origin check.

rules.statement: Serve interactive sign-in, consent and logout pages from the OP's own origin and submit them as native HTML form POSTs that carry the antiforgery token, not as cross-origin or `fetch`-based calls.
rules.why: The cookie, antiforgery token and `ReturnUrl` round trip only works when everything is on the same origin, and the no-JavaScript pages have to work under the bundle.
rules.check: Look for login or consent forms that submit through `fetch`/XHR, are hosted on a separate origin (a dev server or CDN), or skip antiforgery validation on the POST endpoint.

rules.statement: Give the interactive sign-in and consent controls explicit, stable ids (`username`, `password`, `login`, `consent-allow`, `consent-deny`) in both the server-rendered pages and the frontend bundle, and never rely on component-library-generated ids.
rules.why: The OpenID conformance suite's headless browser finds fields by stable id or name, and MUI's generated ids are not stable selectors.
rules.check: Check that a change to a login or consent page or component keeps these exact ids set explicitly and doesn't rename or drop them or leave them to generated ids.

rules.statement: When the user denies consent on the consent page, answer the authorization request with the `access_denied` error.
rules.why: The consent page is a front end over persisted consent, and the decision defines deny as `access_denied`.
rules.check: Look at the consent deny handler and check that it returns an `access_denied` authorization error, not some other error or a silent redirect.

rules.statement: An interactive login must go through the existing authentication challenge and sign-in seam (verify the credential, resolve the principal, check its standing, create the session, then call `SignInAsync`) and must not add a parallel authentication model or session path.
rules.why: The challenge pipeline, the cookie scheme defaults and the credential path have to stay the single route to a session.
rules.check: Look for login code that skips the standing check or session creation, issues its own cookie or ticket outside `SignInAsync`, or adds a new authentication scheme or handler alongside the existing one.

rules.statement: A backend-agnostic capability package must define its backend as an interface in its `.Abstractions` package and must not reference a concrete store or persistence; each concrete backend registers its implementation from its own package.
rules.why: Putting a concrete backend inside the surface package ties it to that store and its persistence and breaks dependency inversion, so alternative backends (LDAP, an external IdP, passwordless) could not plug in.
rules.check: Look for project references or `using` directives in a capability implementation package that point to account stores, EF/persistence packages or concrete backend implementations.

rules.statement: Put a capability in its own leaf package and leave the composition-root/server project to compose it; never implement the capability inline in the composition root.
rules.why: Inlined code can only be referenced by taking the whole server, and its backend ends up hard-wired.
rules.check: Look for new endpoints, handlers, renderers or services implemented directly in the server/composition-root project rather than in a capability package.

rules.statement: An opt-in capability's registration must not register a default backend implementation or turn the capability on by default; the host has to add it and name its backend explicitly.
rules.why: Because the surface is opt-in and wires no backend, a host that enables it must choose a backend, the way the password grant stays unsupported until a capability supplies it.
rules.check: Look for `TryAdd`/`Add` calls that register a default implementation of a backend seam inside the capability's own registration, or for the capability being wired by default in base libraries.

rules.statement: A capability's DI registration extension method must extend the prerequisite library's marker builder (for example `IServiceBuilder<TLibrary>`), not `IServiceCollection`, so the capability cannot be added without its prerequisite.
rules.why: DI registration proves every prerequisite at compile time through marker builders.
rules.check: Look for new `Add*` extension methods for a dependent capability whose `this` parameter is `IServiceCollection` or the wrong marker builder.

rules.statement: Bind a capability's options section strictly, validate it on start, and resolve relative paths in its options against the host content root.
rules.why: The registration binds its configuration section strictly, validates on start and resolves `BundleRootPath` against the content root, so bad configuration fails at startup.
rules.check: Look for options binding without `ValidateOnStart`, binding that silently ignores unknown keys, or relative file paths in options used without resolving them against `IHostEnvironment.ContentRootPath`.

rules.statement: When a capability registers an authentication cookie scheme, register it as a named scheme and never set it as the host's default authentication scheme.
rules.why: The scheme has to match the configured authenticate and challenge scheme names without taking over the host's default authentication.
rules.check: Look for `AddAuthentication(scheme)`, or for `DefaultScheme`/`DefaultChallengeScheme`/`DefaultAuthenticateScheme` being assigned, inside a capability's registration.
